$comment: The capabilities an adapter's emitted artifact actually carries.
`onDemandImages` is whether the deployed function answers `/__ruvyxa/image`.
`onDemandRevalidation` is whether `revalidatePath()` reaches what a visitor
is served. It is false where a cache sits in front of the function and the
adapter has no way to drop one path from it: Firebase Hosting and Amplify's
CloudFront both cache the function's response on the `s-maxage` it sends and
expose no per-path purge to the code running inside. A forced write there
refreshes the function's own store and nothing a reader can see, until the
window expires on its own. It is true where the store the function writes is
the cache a reader is served from (a Worker's KV, a standalone server's
filesystem) and where the adapter implements the platform's purge (Vercel's
`x-prerender-revalidate`, Netlify's `purgeCache` by cache tag).
`ruvyxa build` reports a false against a project that uses ISR or PPR, the
same way it reports an adapter with no image pipeline: a deployment without
instant revalidation is still a valid deployment, and a silent one is not.
`clientIpHeaders` is the header this adapter's own platform ingress writes
*and overwrites*, which the emitted handler passes to `createHandler`. Every
per-client control keys on the answer: the built-in `rate` middleware, the
server-action rate limiter, and the action replay guard's per-client quota.
It is required rather than defaulted, so a new adapter has to decide — the
way `onDemandImages` is. Netlify and Firebase both declared nothing while
having documented ingress of their own, so identity fell through to a
right-to-left scan of `X-Forwarded-For` on platforms whose real client is
not where that scan looks, and every visitor shared one bucket.
An empty list is the correct answer, not a missing one, for the standalone
server the node, bun, deno, aws, railway, and render adapters emit: that is
an ordinary `0.0.0.0` HTTP server with no ingress writing anything, so it
weighs the transport peer against `security.trustedProxyIps` instead.
Declaring a header the platform does not overwrite reintroduces exactly the
bug this mechanism exists to prevent — one client rotating a fabricated
value for a fresh bucket per request — so a value is added only for an
ingress that is documented to overwrite it.
Firebase is empty deliberately and not by oversight: for Cloud Functions v2
the client is the *left* end of `X-Forwarded-For`, the one end the
right-to-left scan will not take, so the fix there is a
`security.trustedProxyIps` guidance change and not a header name.
$conditionalSupportNote: `supports` above is what each adapter declares with no options — which is
